The Ringed caecilian (Siphonops annulatus) is a soil-dwelling amphibian whose life history has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions. Neonates at the moment of hatching measure approximately 4.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 4.5 centimeters] in total length, a value recorded from multiple captive-born clutches. The onset of metamorphosis in this species is marked by a total length of 15 centimeters , at which point the larvae initiate tail resorption and gill regression. This developmental milestone occurs after a period of rapid aquatic growth, during which the endo-trophic tadpoles transition from yolk dependency to active feeding. The total length at birth provides a useful baseline for assessing juvenile growth trajectories, particularly when compared with related gymnophionan species that exhibit similar post-hatching size distributions.

Females of Siphonops annulatus, maintained at a constant 23 °C [T = 23 °C], exhibit a maximum adult size of 48 centimeters [Li = 48 centimeters] in total length, a dimension that represents the upper limit of somatic growth observed in this taxon. Correspondingly, the wet weight of fully grown individuals reaches 116.35 grams [Wwi = 116.35 grams], a body mass associated with reproductively active adults. These ultimate values are derived from a long-term captive colony. Under these stable conditions, juveniles display a consistent growth pattern that culminates in the attainment of these asymptotic measurements. The relatively modest adult body size of this species, compared to some larger caecilian congeners, likely reflects its fossorial habits and the energetic constraints imposed by burrowing through compact tropical soils.

Reproductive output in Siphonops annulatus has been quantified through observations of captive breeding events conducted at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with clutch sizes ranging from 4 to 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 16 eggs per clutch]. This annual reproductive mode is typical of many direct-developing caecilians, where maternal attendance of the egg mass is common. The wet weight of newborns is a modest 0.22 grams [Wwb = 0.22 grams], a remarkably low mass that highlights the substantial parental investment required to nurture the eggs through embryogenesis to hatching. The energetic demands of vitellogenesis and egg brooding likely constrain the frequency of reproductive events, as no female in the study produced more than one clutch within a given calendar year.

Puberty in this species, as inferred from gonadal maturation and the onset of reproductive behavior, is attained when individuals reach a total length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. With a total length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] marking puberty, the caecilian's wet weight at this stage reaches approximately 8.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.4 grams], a mass that signals the transition from juvenile growth to potential reproductive competence. The endpoint of larval development, with a wet weight of roughly 3.6 grams , marks the beginning of a critical feeding period that nearly triples body mass to the pubertal weight of 8.4 grams [Wwp = 8.4 grams], reflecting a phase of intense terrestrial foraging and resource acquisition. This pattern of delayed maturation, with puberty occurring well after metamorphic completion, is consistent with the life-history strategies observed in other fossorial amphibians that require substantial post-metamorphic growth before allocating energy to reproduction.

Longevity data for Siphonops annulatus remain sparse, but captive records maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This estimate, derived from the oldest individuals in the colony, suggests a relatively extended life span compared to many anuran amphibians of similar adult body mass. The ultimate wet weight of 116.35 grams [Wwi = 116.35 grams] is achieved within the first few years of life, after which growth plateaus and somatic maintenance becomes the primary energetic priority. Under optimal captive conditions, these caecilians exhibit low rates of age-related physiological decline, with senescent mortality rarely documented before the eighth year. The correlation between their slow life history, extended longevity of 10 years [am = 10 years], and moderate reproductive output underscores a strategy of steady, iteroparous reproduction rather than a single explosive breeding event at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Continued longitudinal studies will help refine these demographic parameters under varying thermal and dietary regimes.
